title: Wood and Comfort: A Comparative Case Study of Two Multifunctional Rooms
research_question: To determine the impact wooden spaces have on comfort levels by quantitatively and qualitatively comparing thermal, acoustical, and visual parameters in the wood and non-wood rooms.

participants.description: The study involved instrumental measurements and photographic surveys in two existing multifunctional rooms at Laval University, Quebec, Canada. During measurements, only the researcher was present in the rooms.
participants.recruitment: Not applicable, as the study focused on environmental measurements within existing spaces rather than human participants.

stimuli_or_exposures.description:
Two multifunctional rooms at Laval University, Quebec, Canada. 
1. Wood room: 87% indoor wood finishes (yellow birch panels/slats, sugar maple floorboards), located on the second floor of Gene-H.-Kruger Pavilion (built 2004), 204 m², 5.4 m height, 96.7 m² window area (47.4% window-to-floor ratio), North-west orientation. 
2. Non-wood room: <3% indoor wood finishes, located on the fourth floor of Alphonse-Desjardins Pavilion (built 1996), 238 m², 3.4 m height, 42.7 m² window area (17.9% window-to-floor ratio), North-west orientation. Finishes included beige/orange linoleum floor, white perforated steel acoustic ceiling, light grey gypsum walls, black curtain, PVC retractable partition, and small glossy yellow wood panels.

findings.antecedent: Room type (wood room vs. non-wood room)
findings.consequent: Thermal comfort parameters (ambient temperature, surface temperature, operative temperature)
findings.mechanism: Mechanical systems in both rooms likely maintained similar indoor environmental quality within acceptable ranges.
findings.quote: Both rooms could be considered comfortable in relation to the thermal comfort standards defined by ASHRAE and CIBSE

findings.antecedent: Room type (wood room vs. non-wood room)
findings.mechanism: Mechanical systems in both rooms likely maintained similar indoor environmental quality within acceptable ranges.
findings.quote: both rooms share similar thermal and acoustic comfort parameters

findings.antecedent: Room type (wood room vs. non-wood room)
findings.mechanism: The extensive use of wood surfaces in one room versus diverse artificial finishes in the other created distinct visual ambiances.
findings.quote: both rooms share similar thermal and acoustic comfort parameters, but have contrasting visual characteristics.

findings.antecedent: Indoor use of wood (colour, knots, grain)
findings.mechanism: The natural features and yellow-red hue of wood are culturally associated with warmth.
findings.quote: The colour, knots, and grain of the wood contributed to producing visually warm experiences resulting in a yellowish room

findings.mechanism: The diverse range of artificial materials with varying colours and reflectances created a cooler visual impression.
findings.quote: a mix and match of artificial finishes generates a colder, bluish ambiance in the other room.

findings.mechanism: Wood's unique visual ambiances contribute to a sense of warmth and naturalness, which are perceived as comfortable.
findings.quote: architects and designers should consider the indoor use of wood for its unique visual ambiances that enhance comfort levels.

findings.mechanism: Differences in building characteristics (e.g., construction year, volume) and material properties may contribute to temperature variations.
findings.quote: The median ambient temperature in the wood room was 22.7 °C with a humidity level of 44%, while the non-wood room had a higher median temperature (26.2 °C)

findings.mechanism: Differences in building characteristics (e.g., construction year, volume) and material properties may contribute to humidity variations.
findings.quote: The median ambient temperature in the wood room was 22.7 °C with a humidity level of 44%, while the non-wood room had a higher median temperature (26.2 °C) and a lower humidity level (36.1%).

findings.mechanism: The humidity level was below the acceptable CIBSE range, suggesting potential for discomfort.
findings.quote: the humidity level in the non-wood room (36.1%) was below the acceptable CIBSE range (40% to 70%)

findings.mechanism: The larger volume of the wood room (36% larger) likely contributed to lower CO2 concentrations.
findings.quote: The median level observed in the wood room (385 ppm) was 5% lower than the concentration (405 ppm) in the non-wood room.

findings.mechanism: Differences in mechanical and ventilation systems, or material properties, may contribute to noise variations.
findings.quote: The non-wood room showed slightly higher background noise levels (50.0 dBA) than the wood room (48.5 dBA).

findings.mechanism: Larger window area and room height in the wood room contributed to higher luminance values.
findings.quote: The luminance levels recorded in the wood room surpass the levels in the non-wood room (Fig. 5).

findings.mechanism: Larger window area and room height in the wood room contributed to higher luminance values.
findings.quote: In the middle of the wood room, a luminance level of 1772 lux exceeds that nearest the windows in the non-wood room (1603 lux).

findings.mechanism: The large window area and room height in the wood room, rather than interior surfaces, explain the higher daylight factor.
findings.quote: The average daylight factor was 4.4% in the wood room and 1.6% in the non-wood room.

findings.consequent: Light ambiance (uniform, narrower range of colours in false colour images)
findings.mechanism: The uniform reflectance and colour of the wood surfaces contributed to a more consistent light distribution.
findings.quote: the false colour images of the wood room revealed a narrower range of colours. This indicates a uniform light ambiance in the wood room, a feature attributed to the widespread use of yellow birch for the walls and ceiling.

findings.consequent: Light ambiance (large range of colours in false colour images, low luminance on lateral wall)
findings.mechanism: Varying reflectances and colours of different materials (e.g., black curtain, linoleum tiles) created a more diverse light distribution.
findings.quote: In contrast, a large range of colours occurred in the false colour images of the non-wood room. The black curtain on the lateral wall showed low luminance values and thereby contributed to a wide colour range.

findings.mechanism: The software calculation for VCP was more influenced by window location and size than surface reflectance and illumination levels.
findings.quote: The probability of visual comfort in the non-wood room was higher than in the wood room according to the statistical data (Table 3).

findings.mechanism: Viewing away from the window reduces direct glare and improves visual comfort.
findings.quote: The highest visual comfort probability in each conference room was observed for the viewpoint of an occupant with their back to the window (viewpoint 4).

findings.mechanism: Facing the window increases the likelihood of direct glare, reducing visual comfort.
findings.quote: Viewpoint 6, representing occupants facing the window, showed the lowest visual comfort probability in each room.

findings.mechanism: The natural yellow-red hue of wood surfaces contributes to a perception of warmth.
findings.quote: The five selected points in the wood room showed higher b* values than the equivalent points in the non-wood room (Fig. 7). These values indicate a yellowish, warm wood room

findings.mechanism: The diverse range of artificial finishes with cooler hues contributes to a perception of coldness.
findings.quote: in contrast to a bluish, cold non-wood room.

findings.antecedent: Wood room (lateral walls vs. back wall)
findings.mechanism: Variation in natural light reaching surfaces and naturally occurring features (grains, knots) explain colour contrasts within the wood room.
findings.quote: The lateral walls (points 1 and 5) registered similar colour temperatures whereas the back wall (point 3) had a lower b* value, thus less yellow colour temperature.

findings.consequent: Visual experiences (diversity depending on observer distance)
findings.mechanism: The natural textures, knots, and grains of wood reveal more detail upon closer inspection, creating a richer visual experience.
findings.quote: The use of decorative wood panels generated a diversity of visual experiences in the wood room depending on the distance of the observer

findings.mechanism: Wood's inherent material properties result in slower heat transfer, allowing handprints to stay defined longer.
findings.quote: lower conductivity levels in the wood room where the handprint stayed defined. The material's properties determined by previous research support these results. Birch wood shares similar conductivity values (0.17 to 0.18 W/m·K) as maple wood (0.16 to 0.17 W/m·K)

findings.mechanism: These materials' inherent properties result in faster heat transfer, causing handprints to disappear quickly.
findings.quote: In the non-wood room, the researcher's handprint started disappearing from the walls within a few seconds. This suggests a high thermal conductivity for these surfaces

findings.consequent: Comfort levels under cold ambient conditions
findings.mechanism: Higher heat transfer rates mean surfaces rapidly absorb body heat, leading to a colder tactile sensation.
findings.quote: Higher heat transfer rates in the non-wood room could result in lower comfort levels under cold ambient conditions, as the surfaces would rapidly absorb the body's heat.

findings.mechanism: Linoleum's lower specific heat capacity (1.26 kJ/kg·K) compared to hardwood (1.63 kJ/kg·K) means it heats up faster with less heat input.
findings.quote: The infrared thermography of the linoleum floor is yellower, thus warmer, than the other surfaces (Fig. 9). This thermal difference resulted in part from the material's specific heat capacity.

mechanisms: Mechanical systems in both rooms maintained similar indoor environmental quality, leading to similar thermal and acoustic comfort parameters.
The natural colour, knots, and grain of wood contribute to visually warm experiences, aligning with cultural associations of warmth and naturalness.
The diverse range of artificial finishes with varying colours and reflectances creates a colder, bluish visual ambiance.
Larger window areas and room heights significantly influence daylight factor and luminance levels, overriding the impact of interior surface finishes on these metrics.
The location and size of windows have a greater influence on Visual Comfort Probability (VCP) calculations than surface reflectance and illumination levels.
Wood's lower thermal conductivity and higher specific heat capacity result in slower heat transfer, making it feel warmer to the touch and potentially more comfortable in cold conditions.
The natural textures and features of wood (knots, grains) provide a richer, more authentic visual experience that varies with observer distance, unlike uniform artificial surfaces.
moderators: Observer distance (for visual experience of wood textures)
Ambient temperature (for thermal comfort implications of material conductivity)
Window location and size (for Visual Comfort Probability)
Natural light variation (for colour contrasts within wood room)
implementation_implications: Architects and designers should consider the indoor use of wood for its unique visual ambiances that enhance comfort levels.
The visual properties of wood (colour, knots, grain) can create a sense of warmth and naturalness, which can be leveraged in design.
Material selection impacts thermal comfort, with lower thermal conductivity materials like wood potentially offering greater comfort upon contact in colder environments.
While instrumental measures of thermal and acoustic comfort may be similar across different material palettes due to mechanical systems, visual characteristics offer distinct experiences.
Designers should consider material colours and reflectance in addition to textures and physical properties for visual comfort studies, as they significantly impact light distribution and ambiance.

tables.description: Characteristics of the Wood and Non-Wood Multifunctional Rooms, including wood ratio, building, year of construction, room height, room area, window area, window-to-floor ratio, and window orientation.

Acceptable Thresholds for Occupant Comfort in All Room Types according to ASHRAE and CIBSE standards, for parameters like operative temperature, humidity, maximum CO2 concentration, background noise level, and luminance.
Visual Comfort Probabilities (VCP) extracted from Photolux Software for different viewpoints (2, 4, 6) in both the wood and non-wood rooms.

limitations: Additional variables such as contrasting room heights, window areas, and construction years between the two rooms may have influenced the indoor environmental quality and potentially compromised some findings.
The study relied solely on photographic and software analysis for visual ambiances; a subjective evaluation from occupants is needed to complement these findings.
The instrumental measurements were taken by only the researcher, not actual occupants, which limits the direct assessment of occupant comfort perception.

Methodological limitations for the thermal survey include the lack of a predetermined and constant heat source for handprint tests, and the use of a global emissivity value (0.90) for all surfaces, neglecting material particularities.
